ABSTRACT

ENSURING WATER BIOSTABILITY FOR SUSTAINABLE WATER QUALITY: CHALLENGES AND INNOVATIONS IN ENVIRONMENTAL WATER MANAGEMENT

Journal: Journal CleanWAS (JCleanWAS)

Author: Landry S. Omalanga and Ednah K. Onyari

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

Doi: 10.26480/jcleanwas.01.2026.55.62

Maintaining sustainable water quality requires more than just removal of contaminants at the treatment plant; it also requires ensuring that water remains biologically stable (biostable) during storage and distribution. Water biostability refers to the condition in which water does support microbial growth or biofilm formation in drinking water distribution networks (DWDNs). This review aims to combine our understanding of water quality and biostability concepts, discuss the science behind water biostability (nutrients, disinfectant residuals, biofilms, and materials), outline some of the major challenges in water biostability (aging infrastructure, source water variability, climate change, etc.), and finally discuss some recent advances in water biostability monitoring and management. In particular, this review examines case studies and practical applications to illustrate how biostability can be assessed and managed across different stages of water treatment and distribution. Finally, the review identifies gaps and directions for practice, which include the need to monitor microbes in real-time, to use predictive models that integrate hydraulics and microbial ecology, as well as to have regulations that integrate biostability criteria into water quality management for sustainable water supply.
